lineages.name: Arsenio Rodríguez
lineages.why: Developed son montuno in the 1940s: expanded the septeto into the conjunto with three trumpets, piano and conga, and a cowbell in the montuno. He layered interlocking guajeos across instruments and wrote two-celled, clave-specific bass tumbaos that 'sing' — the template salsa inherited.

lineages.name: Eddie Palmieri
lineages.why: His Conjunto La Perfecta (1961) replaced violins with trombones and flute — the 'trombanga' — a heavier, bolder front line later bands copied. Azúcar pa' ti (1965) shows his piano; he later recorded mozambique and Harlem River Drive, and rejected the word 'salsa' as a commercial label.

lineages.name: Johnny Pacheco and Fania Records
lineages.why: Pacheco co-founded Fania in 1964 with Jerry Masucci, first selling records from his car, and in 1968 assembled the Fania All-Stars. The label's roster — Willie Colón, Héctor Lavoe, Rubén Blades, Celia Cruz, Ray Barretto — is the sound the word 'salsa' was coined for; the 1971 Cheetah concert became the film Our Latin Thing.

lineages.name: Willie Colón and Rubén Blades
lineages.why: Colón produced and arranged, Blades wrote: Siembra (1978) became the best-selling salsa album, with long-form narrative songs and social commentary. Colón also produced Lavoe's 'El Cantante', a Blades song running over ten minutes.

name: Salsa / son

notes.text: Clave is the structural core: salsa uses son clave almost exclusively, and every rhythm-section part is written to fit it. Most salsa is phrased 2-3; playing a part against the wrong side of the clave ('cruzado') breaks the groove.

Percussion roles: congas play the tumbao/marcha (slap plus two open tones, heel-toe in between); bongo plays the martillo in verses and switches to the hand bell in the montuno; timbales play cáscara on the shell in quiet sections and the mambo bell in loud ones; maracas and güiro keep the pulse.

The tumbao accents the and-of-2 (bombo) and beat 4 (ponche); the and-of-2 usually carries the fifth and beat 4 anticipates the root of the next bar's chord, so the bass announces each chord change a beat early. Arsenio Rodríguez made the tumbao two-celled and clave-specific, and insisted the bass 'sing'.

The montuno runs over a short vamp — the guajeo literature's standard is I-IV-V-IV, and minor tunes often alternate just i and V. The piano guajeo is a syncopated arpeggiated ostinato, mostly upbeats, often doubled in octaves.

The son montuno model: a verse section (cuerpo), then the montuno — coro-pregón call-and-response — which usually runs to the end, subdivided into mambo, diablo, moña and especial sections and instrumental solos.

evidence.inferred: No source gives bar counts; derived from the two-bar clave cycle the cited sources require every part to respect.

notes.text: Section lengths vary widely by arrangement and live stretching; the bar counts in the form below are an eight-bar-phrase sketch, each phrase an even number of bars so the clave cycle is never cut.

In the montuno the coro has a fixed melody and text, sung in two or three parts moving in parallel; the lead singer answers with improvised pregones (soneos), often with trademark phrases such as Celia Cruz's '¡Azúcar!'.

Horns work in call-and-response mambos and moñas — layered horn guajeos, sometimes improvised — rather than as sustained pads. Romántica is softer; dura and timba want tighter percussion and harder horn stabs.
Line-ups vary: Arsenio Rodríguez's conjunto added a trumpet section, piano and conga to the septeto; Eddie Palmieri's La Perfecta (1961) swapped the violins for trombones and flute (the 'trombanga').

Traditional Latin records are mastered quieter than electronic Latin pop and draw their punch from the mid-range, where most of the energy sits; transient shaping there is preferred over heavy limiting.
Fania-era salsa carried narrative and social commentary as well as dance texts: Siembra's 'Pedro Navaja' is modelled on Brecht's Threepenny Opera and 'Plástico' satirizes consumerism.

Tempo counting is disputed: dancers count 160–220 BPM in quarter notes, but players often feel the music in half time (~90), which is why the montuno and tumbao do not sound frantic. A groove written in 4/4 at ~95 BPM with the tumbao on the and-of-2 and 4 is the same music read at half speed only if the whole clave fits in one bar.

pitfalls.text: Writing the bass on the downbeat like rock or pop. The tumbao lands on the and-of-2 and on 4, anticipating the next chord's root; beat 1 is usually tied over, not struck.
Playing the piano montuno 'cruzado' — aligned to the wrong side of the clave. Decide 2-3 or 3-2 first and lock every part to it.
Using horns as continuous pads. Write call-and-response mambo and moña figures instead, and leave the percussion room to breathe.

progressions.text: The standard montuno/guajeo vamp, one pass per clave cycle.

A four-chord montuno used in more contemporary tunes.

evidence.inferred: The cited tumbao puts one attack on the and-of-2 and one on 4 per 4/4 bar (Wikipedia 'Tumbao', Rhythm Notes); the third allows for the double ponche Ian Stewart and others describe as variation.
In the cited basic tumbao one of the two attacks (the and-of-2) is off the quarter grid and one (beat 4) is on it, giving 0.5; the range allows for pushed variations and for extra on-beat notes.
The cited tumbao anticipates the next bar's root on beat 4 and ties it over, so beat 1 is normally not re-struck (Wikipedia 'Tumbao': the bass emphasizes offbeats rather than downbeats).
The anticipated root on 4 is held over the bar line into the next and-of-2 in the cited tumbao, so notes fill almost all of the space to the next attack.

evidence.inferred: The cited montuno vamps are two-bar patterns aligned to the clave: I-IV-V-IV across two bars is two chords a bar; the two-chord minor vamp (Cm-G) is one a bar.
Counting root motion in the cited vamps: I-IV-V-IV has two fourth/fifth moves out of four (0.5); i-V alternation is all fifths (1.0).

summary: Dance music built on the son montuno model: every rhythm-section part is written to fit a two-bar son clave, the bass plays an anticipated tumbao on the and-of-2 and on 4, and the piano plays a syncopated guajeo (montuno). A short sung verse gives way to a long call-and-response montuno section, broken up by horn mambos and moñas.
